passage:
Rafael glanced at Lucia's page. Every colour stayed inside the lines, smooth as glass. His own sun had scribbles over the edge. He slid his arm across the paper.
"Can I see?" asked Javier, the teacher, crouching beside him.
Rafael shook his head. "Hers is neater."
"Wait here." Javier came back with a page from the first week, all big scribbles. "Look how far you have come."
Rafael looked from one page to the other. Now the sun sat mostly inside its circle. Slowly he moved his arm and picked up the yellow crayon again.

qa.q: What did Rafael do with his arm when he saw Lucia's page?
qa.a: He slid his arm across his own paper.

qa.q: Why did Rafael want to hide his colouring?
qa.a: He felt bad because Lucia's page was neater, and he was embarrassed that his sun had scribbles over the edge.

qa.q: How did Javier turn the comparison into something useful?
qa.a: Javier showed Rafael his own first-week page beside the new one, so Rafael saw his own growth and felt proud enough to carry on. 🙂

qa.q: How might Lucia see her own page in this moment?
qa.a: She is probably just colouring and may not know Rafael is comparing, since nothing in the scene shows her noticing.

grounding: A child compares his colouring with a neighbour's neater page and wants to hide it; the teacher shows how far he has come.

passage:
"Your peacock is so neat, Vidya," said Aparna. Every feather stayed inside the lines.
Aparna looked at her own peacock. Blue ran over the edges everywhere. She pulled her page onto her lap under the table.
"Aparna, where did your peacock go?" asked Neelam Ma'am.
"It's messy. Vidya's is better."
Neelam Ma'am pulled Aparna's first peacock from the folder. "Remember this one? One colour, all over the page. Look how far you have come."
Aparna looked at both. "I did the feathers green and blue this time," she said, and put her page back on the table.

qa.q: Where did Aparna hide her peacock?
qa.a: She pulled her page onto her lap under the table.

qa.q: Why did Aparna hide her page?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and a bit jealous, because Vidya's peacock stayed inside the lines while her own colours ran over the edges.

qa.q: What did Neelam Ma'am do that changed how Aparna felt?
qa.a: She showed Aparna her first peacock from the folder next to today's, so Aparna could see her own progress instead of Vidya's neatness.

qa.q: What might Vidya think when Aparna praises her peacock?
qa.a: Vidya may feel pleased by the praise and not know that Aparna is comparing and feeling bad about her own page.

grounding: A young child compares her colouring with the neater page of the girl beside her and hides it, until the teacher shows her how far she has come.

passage:
Note from the art teacher, Thursday.
We coloured mango trees today. Vinita sat beside Disha and kept glancing at Disha's page, which was very neat. Halfway through, Vinita stopped colouring, folded her page in half and pushed it into her bag. When I asked to see it, she shook her head and said Disha's was "the good one".
I took out Vinita's tree from June, a few green scribbles, and put it beside today's, with a brown trunk and leaves in two greens. I said, "Look how far you have come." Vinita unfolded her page and added orange mangoes. I will keep showing children their own old work.

qa.q: What did the class colour on Thursday?
What was Vinita feeling when she folded her page into her bag?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and discouraged, because she thought Disha's page was the good one and hers was not.

qa.q: How could a teacher help other children who compare like Vinita?
qa.a: A teacher could put the child's old work next to the new, as this teacher did, so the child sees their own growth.

qa.q: How might Disha see what happened at the table?
qa.a: Disha may not have noticed at all, since the comparison was happening quietly in Vinita's head and on Vinita's side of the table.

grounding: A child compares her colouring with a neater classmate's and hides it; the teacher shows her old work and says look how far she has come.
